newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE-Albania, which hated foreigners, now wants them.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Albania, which hated foreigners, now wants them.

text.p: After trying to keep foreigners out of the country for 40 years, Albania is now desperately trying to get them in.

Conscious that tourism offers the best prospects for economic growth in Europe's poorest state after four decades of Stalinist rule, it has been working hard on promoting itself since the fall of communism in 1990.

This is in stark contrast to the isolationism of late dictator Enver Hoxha, who after falling out with the rest of the world built 700,000 concrete bunkers across the country to keep out overland visitors and spike-topped concrete pillars to deter those landing by parachute.

With more than 300 km (170 miles) of spectacular Adriatic coastline and 2,400 hours of sunshine each year, similar to Greece, Albania should be well placed to take a decent share of the international holiday market.

It also has a wealth of historic buildings and ancient Greek and Roman archaeological sites, although a number of historical museums were looted and vandalised in an orgy of violence during an uprising last March.

For nature lovers, the mountainous north, which has been virtually cut off from the rest of Europe for decades, contains some of Europe's last wild habitats for wolves, jackals, bears and lynx, and the eagle which features in the national flag.
"A BIT OF AN IMAGE PROBLEM"

But just as Albania was starting to make modest progress in tourism, a violent rebellion swept the country earlier this year, sparked by the collapse of pyramid savings schemes, leaving hundreds of buildings gutted and vandalised.

With a million looted guns in private hands and most of the south in the control of armed gangs, the country suffers from what one Western diplomat, with masterly understatement, described as "a bit of an image problem".

The downside also extends to infrastructure, as the country where private motoring was banned under the communists now has some of the worst roads in Europe following an explosion of car ownership, and a national water and power system that is creaking under the strain.
UPGRADING INFRASTRUCTURE

Tourism Minister Vasillaq Spaho, who is about to leave the government after ex-communist Socialists won recent elections, agreed that investment in infrastructure was the top priority after the restoration of law and order.

"We can't pretend we can develop tourism, or any other sector of the economy, without improving the infrastructure," he told Reuters, adding that this could take up to 10 years and would inevitably require outside financial assistance.

He said that, before the latest troubles, foreign consultants backed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) had drawn up a long-term programme for "eco-tourism" based on low-rise accommodation which would provide 60,000 new beds for up to a million tourists a year by the year 2010.
This would be a huge leap from last year's figure of just 60,000 tourists, half of them day-trippers from the Greek holiday island of Corfu, close to the southern Albanian port of Sarande.
INVESTMENT INCENTIVES

Four years ago, the government introduced new legislation offering incentives such as five-year tax holidays and a three-year amnesty for paying duty on imported construction materials and equipment for foreign firms.
While welcoming these developments, some foreign firms said there were problems with the regulations.

A Kuwaiti-based company building a tourist complex near the port of Durres, some 40 km (25 miles) from Tirana, as well as running the state airline and building a five-star hotel in the capital, objected to paying value added tax for work under construction.
"The government said the tax would be refunded, but later they said they didn't have enough funds to do it," Zakaria Rashed of Mak Albania, an offshoot of the M.A. Kharafi group, told Reuters.
He also said the government needed to be more generous in compensating developers for providing infrastructure in areas where none existed, which could amount to 25 percent of any project.

"The new government must look at the investment laws if it wants to attract foreign money," he added. "But restoring public order is the first priority. People must be persuaded that they don't need their looted guns to protect themselves."
His company is taking no chances at the luxury villa complex it is building just along the coast from here, hiring a 30-strong security force armed with automatic weapons.

Further down the coast, on a beach that stretches as far as the eye can see, ingenious local entrepreneurs have built cafes on the most unlikely sites -- one on top of a concrete bunker, another on a beached shipwreck.
"I think there is tremendous potential for tourism in Albania, but tourism is a tremendously sensitive industry," a Western economist who asked to be nameless said.
"I think it is very hard to see in the short term how tourists will be lured back to Albania -- but people have quite short memories."
